newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain's Labour Party coy on taxes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain's Labour Party coy on taxes.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party said on Wednesday its present political programme did not imply any increase in personal taxes, but it declined to rule out the possibility that taxes might rise.
"Nothing in this programme implies rises in personal taxation," party leader Tony Blair told a news conference at which he presented a policy document entitled "Leading Britain into the Future."
"There are no uncosted or unfunded spending proposals, no concealed tax increases. Where we plan to spend money, we say where it comes from. There is no evasion, no double dealing, no hidden agenda."

But when pressed to disclose whether the top rate of personal tax would be left unchanged at 40 percent, Blair and finance spokesman Gordon Brown declined to say explicitly that it would not rise. "If there are any changes to our plans, we will tell you," Blair said.
Asked if Labour might contemplate changes in indirect taxes such as value added tax (VAT), Brown said: "We have no wish to put up VAT."
Labour, which has been in opposition since 1979, has been working hard to convince voters ahead of the looming general election that its days as the party of high taxation are over.

A general election is due by May 22 but Prime Minister John Major could be forced to call one sooner following the loss of his parliamentary majority last month. He has said he will call a poll no later than May 1.

The Conservative government, which is well behind the opposition in opinion polls, says Labour's sums do not add up and it would have to increase taxes to finance extra spending in areas such as health and education.

"Mr Blair has concealed the details of how his policies will work," Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney said on Wednesday. "He won't even answer the basic economic questions. He's trying to con you."
Blair denounced as "completely and totally false" Conservative accusations that Labour's programme implied billions of pounds of extra spending. "That whole Tory case is a lie," he said.
The policy document said Labour would be the party of sound finance, tough on public spending and with a rigorous inflation target.
Raising standards in education would be its number one priority. It also aimed to start reforming the welfare state and build a new partnership with business and industry.
Brown said much of this could be done by using existing resources more effectively, such as by spending more on medical staff in the national health service and less on administrators.

The key to reforming the welfare state was tackling youth and long-term unemployment, which would be done through special programmes financed by a windfall levy on the profits of privatised utility companies, the document said.
